subsection: 2. Economic planning and the move to free trade; case study: the First Programme for Economic Expansion, 1958–1963

notes.h: Key concepts: planning, free trade, protectionism and the balance of payments
notes.b: Four ideas run through this subsection. Together they describe the shift from a closed, state-shielded economy to one that planned for growth and competed abroad.
points: Economic planning means the government sets targets for several years ahead and directs public investment and incentives towards them, so that growth is pursued on purpose rather than left to chance. The First Programme was Ireland's first plan of this kind.

Protectionism is the use of tariffs (taxes on imported goods) and controls to shield home industry from foreign competition. Fianna Fáil used it from the 1930s in the hope of making Ireland more self-sufficient.

Free trade is the removal of tariffs and other barriers between countries, so that firms sell across borders on equal terms. It is the opposite of protection, and Ireland moved towards it in the 1960s.

The balance of payments is the gap between what a country earns abroad, mainly from exports, and what it spends abroad on imports. A deficit (spending more than it earns) forced governments to cut back at home, so it shaped policy throughout the period.
notes.tip: If a question asks for a definition, give each concept in a line and tie it to an Irish example, such as the Control of Manufactures Acts for protection or the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement for free trade.

notes.h: Case study background: why protection and drift ended
notes.b: By 1957 the policy of protection that Fianna Fáil had begun in the 1930s was widely seen to have run out of steam. Small factories, one export customer and mass emigration showed that the economy was not growing.
points: Tariffs and the Control of Manufactures Acts of 1932 and 1934 had created many small factories that sold only on the home market. The home market was too small to support efficient industry, so firms stayed small and costly to run.

The Control of Manufactures Acts required that a majority of the shares in a new company (51 per cent) be held by Irish citizens. This discouraged foreign firms from setting up in Ireland, since they could not keep control of their own businesses.
Exports were mostly live cattle and farm produce sold to Britain, so the economy depended on one customer and on farming.
Net emigration in the 1950s was about 400,000 (over the decade 1951–61), and the population fell to about 2.82 million in 1961, while the rest of western Europe was growing fast.
Balance of payments crises in 1951–52 and 1955–56 were met by deflation (cutting spending and demand to reduce imports). This cut demand without improving productive capacity.
Because each crisis was met by deflation and then by recovery, the economy moved in a repeating stop-go pattern. There is more on this in the notes on the alternating governments of 1948–59.

Fianna Fáil returned to government in March 1957, with Seán Lemass at Industry and Commerce (and as Tánaiste, the deputy head of government) and James Ryan at Finance. They were ready to listen to new ideas from officials.
notes.tip: Be ready to say why protection ended, using the small home market, dependence on Britain, emigration and the stop-go crises. Do not confuse the 1957 return to government with Lemass becoming Taoiseach, which came in 1959.

notes.h: Case study: T.K. Whitaker and Economic Development, 1958
notes.b: Economic Development was a study by civil servants, led by Whitaker, that changed the direction of policy. It is the link between the failure of the 1950s and the First Programme.
points: Thomas Kenneth Whitaker became Secretary of the Department of Finance (its top civil servant) in 1956 at the age of 39. He gathered a group of younger officials to examine the economy, and the department that had long resisted spending changed its attitude.

Economic Development was written in the Department of Finance under Whitaker. It was completed in May 1958 and submitted to Ministers, and it was published to the public later in 1958, around the time of the Programme.
It argued that protection had failed to produce growth or jobs, and that emigration was a symptom of an economy that was not expanding.

It recommended shifting public investment from social projects such as housing and hospitals towards directly productive investment in agriculture, industry and tourism, because these would create the jobs and income that pay for social services later.
It welcomed foreign capital and technology, a break with the Control of Manufactures Acts, and it argued for export-led growth (growth driven by selling more abroad).

The government accepted its analysis, and in November 1958 it published the Programme for Economic Expansion, usually called the First Programme, which turned the proposals into a policy with targets.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two documents. Economic Development was the Finance Department's analysis, completed in May 1958. The Programme for Economic Expansion was the government's own plan, published in November 1958.

notes.h: Case study: aims and measures of the First Programme
notes.b: The First Programme ran for five years, from 1959 to 1963, and set out an agenda for growth. Its measures aimed to attract investment and to reward firms that sold abroad.
points: Aim: to raise national output and living standards and to halt emigration, because jobs in export industry and farming would give people a reason to stay.

Target: a rise of about 2 per cent a year in gross national product (the total value of what the country's people produce). It was set deliberately modest, so that it could be achieved and confidence rebuilt.

The Industrial Development (Encouragement of External Investment) Act 1958 ended the rule that Irish citizens must hold most of the shares in new firms, so it opened the way to foreign-owned factories.

Export Profits Tax Relief, which exempted profits from increased exports from tax, was introduced in 1956 by the Second Inter-Party Government. Fianna Fáil kept it and widened it, so it began before the Programme.

The Industrial Development Authority (IDA), set up in 1949, was given a larger role and larger grants in the late 1950s to firms setting up new plant. Incentives favoured less developed areas, such as the west.
The Shannon Free Airport Development Company was set up in 1959 and built an industrial estate at Shannon to attract foreign firms.
In agriculture, An Foras Talúntais (the agricultural research institute) was set up in 1958, and farmers were encouraged to raise productivity and exports.
The state shifted its capital spending (spending on lasting assets such as roads and equipment) towards productive investment, though spending on housing and health rose again as growth took hold.
notes.tip: If asked for the main features of the Programme, give the modest target, the ending of the foreign-ownership rule, export tax relief, IDA grants and productive public investment. Remember that Export Profits Tax Relief began under the Inter-Party government, not under the Programme.

notes.h: Case study: results against the targets
notes.b: Judged by its own targets, the First Programme succeeded, and it did so by a wide margin. The results are best shown as target against outcome, with the limits and the outside help set beside them.
points: Real national output grew by about 4 per cent a year between 1958 and 1963, about double the 2 per cent target and faster than in the previous decade.
Exports of manufactured goods rose sharply, and industrial production grew because new, mostly foreign-owned firms began to operate.
Net emigration fell to about 80,000 in 1961–66, from about 200,000 in 1956–61, so the haemorrhage of people had slowed.
Because emigration slowed, the 1966 census recorded a population of about 2.88 million, up from about 2.82 million in 1961. This was the first rise since the early 1950s.
Unemployment fell but remained a serious problem, and total employment barely rose because jobs in farming continued to decline.
The balance of payments remained fragile, and by the mid-1960s wage claims and inflation were raising difficulties.
Part of the success lay outside Ireland. The late 1950s and 1960s were years of strong growth in Britain and Europe, which raised the demand for Irish exports.
notes.tip: Use the target of about 2 per cent against the result of about 4 per cent, then the limits (employment, balance of payments) and the outside boom. Do not swap the First Programme's targets with the Second Programme's.

notes.h: Case study: significance and differing views
notes.b: Historians agree that the First Programme mattered, but they disagree about how much of the change it caused. The question is whether it was a turning point or part of a longer story.
points: The Programme was the start of regular economic planning in Ireland, so it was followed by a Second Programme published in 1963 and a Third Programme covering 1969–72.
Contemporaries welcomed it as a sharp break with the pessimism of the 1950s. The idea of a plan for growth was supported across the parties and by the trade unions and employers.
Those who see it as a turning point stress the end of protection, the openness to foreign investment and the change in public confidence.

Sceptical historians stress that the world economy was booming, which lifted Irish exports whatever the policy. They add that the Programme built on measures begun by the Inter-Party governments, such as Export Profits Tax Relief, and that its targets were modest.
Critics on the left argued that foreign firms took profits out of the country, so Ireland kept less of the gain, and that growth was uneven, with the west benefiting least.
Whitaker himself stressed that the Programme was a framework, and that its success depended on private investors and on a favourable international climate.
notes.tip: For contemporary against later views, pair the praise at the time with the later debate over policy against the world boom. Name continuity evidence such as Export Profits Tax Relief to show you know the sceptics' case.

notes.b: Lemass became Taoiseach (head of government) in June 1959, when de Valera was elected President, and he carried the Programme through. His record is a mix of modernizing steps and unfinished business.
points: Lemass became Taoiseach on 23 June 1959 and held the office until 10 November 1966, when Jack Lynch succeeded him. He had been a minister since 1932 and was a pragmatic modernizer.
His style was practical, businesslike and impatient for change, in contrast to de Valera, the older leader he succeeded.

He built closer links with the trade unions and employers, called social partnership, so that pay could be settled by agreement. The national wage rounds, in which unions, employers and the government bargained over general pay increases, began in 1964.

The government set up the Committee on Industrial Organisation in the early 1960s and, from 1963, adaptation councils to help industries prepare for competition from free trade, since protected firms would soon lose their tariff shelter.

The Second Programme for Economic Expansion, published in 1963, aimed for growth of about 4 per cent a year to 1970, but it was abandoned in 1967 after wage rises and a balance of payments deficit. A Third Programme followed for 1969–72.
He used the new television service, Telefís Éireann, to explain government policy and to project an image of a modern state. There is more on this in the RTÉ case study.
He is also remembered for easing the state's attitude to Northern Ireland, as in his 1965 meetings with Terence O'Neill, who was Prime Minister of Northern Ireland.
notes.tip: For the commonest essay, give a stated judgement and balance achievements (planning and growth, social partnership, the EEC application, free trade, the O'Neill meetings) against limits (the abandoned Second Programme, employment, wage claims, partition), with dates.

notes.h: The move to free trade and the EEC
notes.b: Lemass saw that the future of Irish industry lay in competing in open markets, not in protection. Britain was both the main customer and the key to any trade deal.
points: Ireland applied to join the European Economic Community (EEC, the common market of western European states) on 31 July 1961, nine days before Britain did, because Britain was the market for most Irish exports.

President de Gaulle of France vetoed British entry on 14 January 1963, which ended the negotiations for the time being. Ireland's application was blocked with Britain's. There is more on this in the notes on the UN and the EEC.
With EEC entry delayed, Lemass turned to a trade agreement with Britain. The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement was signed on 14 December 1965 and took effect on 1 July 1966.
The agreement removed tariffs on trade between the two countries over ten years and kept access for Irish farm exports to the British market.

Free trade threatened protected Irish firms in textiles, footwear and other consumer goods, and many small firms closed over the next decade, because they could not match foreign prices once the tariffs fell.
Supporters argued that free trade would bring cheaper inputs, larger markets and new investment, and that protected industries could not survive in the long run.

Ireland joined the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT, an international agreement to lower tariffs) in 1967, the year after Lemass left office. It was the end point of the move to lower tariffs, not an act of his government.
Lemass visited Terence O'Neill at Stormont on 14 January 1965, and O'Neill visited Dublin on 9 February 1965. These were the first meetings between the heads of the two governments since the 1920s.
notes.tip: Keep the trade steps separate. The EEC application was in 1961 and was blocked by de Gaulle's veto of Britain, the Free Trade Agreement of 1965–66 was with Britain only, and GATT membership in 1967 came after Lemass had retired.

notes.b: Whitaker was a civil servant, not a politician, and the most influential public official of his generation. He supplied the ideas behind the First Programme.
points: Whitaker was born in 1916 in Rostrevor, Co. Down, and joined the civil service in 1934.
As Secretary of the Department of Finance from 1956 to 1969 he was the main author of Economic Development and the First Programme, working with Lemass and with ministers such as James Ryan.

He shaped events by using the authority of the Department of Finance, which had traditionally resisted spending, to argue for investment. This carried weight because Finance had always been the department that said no.

He later served as Governor of the Central Bank from 1969 to 1976, as a senator from 1977 to 1982 and as chairman of several commissions, including the Constitution Review Group of the mid-1990s. He died in 2017 at the age of 100.
As author of the report, he was a participant in events. He later said that he and his colleagues did the work without extra pay.
Contemporaries praised his clarity and courage in questioning protection, though some in his own department doubted how far growth could be planned.

Historians see him as the architect of the new approach, while stressing that Lemass and de Valera supplied the political will. Some argue that his role has been overstated by the idea that planning alone made the economy grow.
notes.tip: For a short paragraph on Whitaker, give his post and date (Secretary of the Department of Finance, 1956), what Economic Development argued, the plan that followed and one result. Do not call him a minister.

notes.b: Lemass was the minister and then Taoiseach who turned the new thinking into government policy. He is unusual because he built the system of protection and then helped to end it.
points: Lemass was born in Dublin in 1899, fought in the Rising in 1916 and on the anti-Treaty side in the Civil War, and his brother Noel was killed in 1923.
He co-founded Fianna Fáil in 1926. He was Minister for Industry and Commerce from 1932 to 1939, 1941 to 1948, 1951 to 1954 and 1957 to 1959, and Minister for Supplies from 1939 to 1945.

As the architect of the protectionist industrial policy of the 1930s, he was able later to argue that protection had served its purpose and should now give way to competition. The failure of protection had convinced a former protectionist.
As Taoiseach he backed the First Programme because he now believed in growth through exports, applied to join the EEC and signed the Free Trade Agreement.
Contemporaries saw him as a practical, impatient leader who got things done, so he was respected for results, though some in Fianna Fáil mistrusted his break with protection.
Historians and biographers judge him a modernizer who changed the tone of Irish politics, but they note that he left rural poverty, urban housing problems and partition unresolved.
notes.tip: Do not call Lemass Taoiseach in 1958. He was Minister for Industry and Commerce then, and became Taoiseach in June 1959. For a short answer, give when and why he became Taoiseach and one contrast with de Valera.

notes.h: Assessment: Whitaker and Lemass compared, and the First Programme
notes.b: The change of direction needed both an adviser with ideas and a leader with the will to act. The achievements and limits below give the material for a balanced judgement.
points: Whitaker supplied the analysis and Lemass the political leadership. The Programme needed both, and their partnership is the central reason for the change of direction.
Compared directly, Whitaker was a civil servant and Lemass a politician. Whitaker was cautious and analytical by temperament, and Lemass was driven and impatient for results.
Achievements of the First Programme: growth about twice the target, so it beat its aim, falling emigration, rising exports, a shift in confidence and the habit of planning.

Limits: total employment barely increased because farm jobs kept falling, farming and the west lagged, the balance of payments remained fragile and wage claims raised inflation. The Second Programme was abandoned in 1967, and partition and rural poverty were left unresolved.
Contemporary view: the Programme was a success, which is why Fianna Fáil did well in the 1965 election and stayed in office.
Later view: historians accept that it was a turning point but debate how much of the growth came from policy and how much from the European boom.
notes.tip: On a question about both men, compare them directly rather than in two separate lists. Say what each contributed (analysis against political leadership) and show how they combined, ending with a stated judgement.

keyTerms.definition: A policy of setting targets for national output and investment over a number of years and directing public spending and incentives to meet them.
A policy of removing tariffs and other barriers so that goods and investment can move freely between countries.
The 1958 report, prepared in the Department of Finance under T.K. Whitaker, that argued for productive investment and export-led growth.
The five-year plan published in November 1958 to cover 1959–1963, with the target of about 2 per cent growth a year.
The 1932 and 1934 laws that required Irish citizens to hold most of the shares in new manufacturing firms, which discouraged foreign investment until they were ended.
The use of tariffs and import controls to shield home industry from foreign competition.
The agreement of December 1965, in force from July 1966, that removed tariffs on trade between Ireland and Britain over ten years.
A tax concession, introduced in 1956 and extended in 1958, that exempted profits from increased exports from tax.
A national bargaining round in which unions and employers settled a general level of pay increases, often with the government's involvement.
